rows.name: multipart-pause-1500
rows.question: For exactly ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block, compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element. Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounds check. Explain the arithmetic.
rows.recognizedQuestion: For example, ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounce check Explain the arithmetic
rows.answer:
You need 53 blocks, with 16 active threads in the final block and 176 excess threads that must be guarded out. I’m interpreting “bounce check” as “bounds check.”

The block count is ceiling(10,000 / 192): 52 blocks cover 52 × 192 = 9,984 elements, leaving 16, so you need one more block. Launching 53 blocks creates 53 × 192 = 10,176 threads; subtracting 10,000 gives 176 threads with no valid element to process. Normally all 10,176 threads evaluate a guard such as `if (idx < 10000)`, but only those final 176 threads fail it and skip the work.

rows.name: switch-topic
rows.question: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.answer:
Snapshot isolation makes each transaction atomic, but it does not make concurrent transactions behave as though they ran serially. Both transactions can read the same old snapshot, pass the same check, and update different rows, so neither triggers a write-write conflict—even though their combined changes violate an invariant.

For example, suppose Alice and Bob are both on call, and at least one must remain on call. Each transaction reads that both are on call; one sets Alice off call, while the other sets Bob off call. Because they write different rows, both can commit under snapshot isolation, leaving nobody on call.

Atomicity guarantees that each transaction’s changes happen all together or not at all; it does not protect the assumptions established by its reads from concurrent changes. Prevent this with serializable isolation, or by making both transactions acquire a common lock or update a shared guard row before checking the invariant.
